taxonomic_note: Current Kew accepts the species with three subspecies. The learner stays at species rank because Hays/Travis/Williamson records span differing subspecific treatments.
look_here_first: FLIP A LEAF first: glossy green on top, woolly/felted gray-to-tawny beneath (often stronger on young leaves). Follow an entire smooth-edged leaf to the alternate stem; leaves can cluster on spur shoots and look whorled. Examine short shoots for rigid spine-like tips. Then seek tiny creamy flowers in fascicles or oblong blackish fleshy fruit. Do not demand thorns on every shoot.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays project wild-observation pool + Travis herbarium record within the S. lanuginosum complex + Williamson County subsp. oblongifolium treatment.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Species-level learner retained while local subspecific concepts remain historically variable.

best_field_traits: some short shoots terminate in sharp spine-like tips
young lower leaf surface woolly/tomentose, often tawny
older upper leaf surface glossier and less hairy
small flowers in fascicles from short shoots
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Look for woolly/tawny leaf undersides plus spine-like short shoots on an alternate-leaved woody plant.

confused_with: Other thorny woody Central Texas shrubs
comparisons.key_distinctions: First flip a leaf: alternate entire glossy green above, pale tawny or gray woolly beneath (especially young), often crowded on short shoots. Seek stiff spine-like short shoot ends. S. celastrinum has generally smooth undersides and smaller leaves (per Texas A&M Forest Service); Texas persimmon lacks these hard spines and has prominent persisting fruit calyx and smooth peeling trunk bark; possumhaw holly has often finely-toothed leaves and red/orange fruits. Leaf tuft alone may look whorled but actual full shoot attachment is alternate.
